issues.legal_issue: An order made on an application modifying a scheme that forms part of a civil decree is appealable as an amended decree.
material_facts: A scheme for the administration of a religious institution had been framed in a suit and confirmed on appeal, making the scheme part of the decree in that suit.
A later application under the applicable endowments legislation sought modification of the scheme, and the District Judge made an order modifying it.
An appeal was brought to the High Court from the District Judge’s order.
issues.conclusion: The appeal to the High Court was competent because an order modifying the scheme was an amended decree appealable under the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(2) and 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an adjudication modifying a scheme that forms part of a decree is itself an amended decree and is appealable. Sections 75 and 57(9) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927 treated the scheme framed in the suit as a scheme under that Act and provided for its modification or cancellation by application. The Court distinguished Rajagopala Chettiar v. Hindu Religious Endowments Board, I.L.R. 57 Mad. 271 (F.B.), which concerned an application to challenge a Board decision rather than an application to alter a scheme that was part of a decree.

predicates.scheme_modification_proceeding: The proceeding is an application to modify or cancel a scheme governing an institution.
predicates.scheme_part_of_decree: The scheme was framed in a suit and formed part of the decree in that suit.
predicates.court_order_changes_scheme: A court order modifies or cancels the scheme.

issues.definition: When an application in a scheme-modification proceeding results in a court changing a scheme that forms part of a decree, an appeal lies against that order.

issues.legal_issue: A court may not restrict customary remuneration under a scheme on grounds that were not raised in the pleadings or supported by the facts.
material_facts: The existing scheme allowed the archakas customary remuneration, including a share of offerings and other customary emoluments and perquisites.
The Board’s application accepted the archakas’ entitlement to a share of the collections in the offering box and sought to exclude other remuneration, including a share in certain offerings.

The District Judge maintained the existing customary remuneration, but the Board’s appeal did not challenge the archakas’ entitlement to a share in those offerings on the ground that the scheme’s description of their other emoluments was vague.

The High Court restricted the archakas’ remuneration because the reference to other customary emoluments was, in its view, too vague and likely to cause difficulty; the scheme had operated for many years without such difficulty, and the relevant entitlements had been established in prior contested proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to restrict the archakas’ remuneration on the ground of vagueness, and the District Judge’s provision preserving their customary remuneration was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 57(9) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927 provided for modification of a scheme on an application. Section 79 protected established usage and customary rights, honours, emoluments and perquisites, subject to the Act. A court deciding a requested modification may not grant a restriction on a ground not raised in the pleadings or appeal, particularly where the customary rights had been established in prior proceedings and the existing scheme had operated without the alleged difficulty. The Court also recognized that a radical change in circumstances could justify revising remuneration, but no such basis was established here.

predicates.scheme_modification_proceeding: The proceeding is an application to modify a scheme governing an institution.
predicates.customary_remuneration_was_previously_re: The officeholders’ customary remuneration had been recognized in prior contested proceedings and provided for under the existing scheme.
predicates.existing_scheme_operated_without_difficu: The existing scheme had operated for a substantial period without the alleged ambiguity causing difficulty.
predicates.restriction_based_on_unpleaded_vagueness: The court restricted customary remuneration because the scheme’s description was vague, although that basis was not raised in the relevant pleadings or appeal.

issues.definition: If a scheme-modification proceeding concerns customary remuneration previously recognized under a scheme that operated without difficulty, a restriction based on vagueness not raised in the pleadings is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A court may not effectively abolish a hereditary office and deprive its holder of customary remuneration when the application sought only to regulate remuneration if duties were delegated to a deputy.
material_facts: The Karnam held a hereditary office and received customary remuneration for duties connected with the institution’s collections.
The Board complained that the Karnam used deputies whose work was inadequate and sought a reduction in his remuneration if he employed a deputy.
The application did not seek abolition of the office or deprivation of the Karnam’s customary remuneration when he performed the duties himself.
The District Judge required the Karnam to perform the duties personally to receive the customary remuneration and permitted a deputy, subject to approval, when necessary.
The High Court instead provided a fixed salary and allowed the Karnam to appoint a deputy, thereby depriving him of his customary remuneration even if he performed the duties personally.
An executive officer had been assigned some accounting responsibilities, but the Karnam’s customary duties had not thereby been eliminated.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to deprive the Karnam of his customary remuneration and effectively abolish his office; the District Judge’s provision was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 57(9) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927 provided for modification of a scheme on an application, and section 79 addressed established usage and customary rights. The Court held that the relief sought concerned the Karnam’s remuneration when duties were delegated, not abolition of his hereditary office or deprivation of his customary remuneration when he served personally. A court may not grant that broader relief when it was not sought. Assigning some accounting responsibilities to an executive officer did not by itself justify reducing the Karnam’s remuneration to a nominal amount. The Court expressed no opinion on whether, or in what circumstances, the hereditary office could be abolished.

rule.if: scheme_modification_proceeding and hereditary_office_exists and application_did_not_seek_abolition and officeholder_performs_customary_duties and some_responsibilities_assigned_elsewhere

predicates.scheme_modification_proceeding: The proceeding is an application to modify a scheme governing an institution.
predicates.hereditary_office_exists: The officeholder holds the office by hereditary right.
predicates.application_did_not_seek_abolition: The application sought to regulate remuneration in specified circumstances but did not seek abolition of the office or deprivation of customary remuneration for personal service.
predicates.officeholder_performs_customary_duties: The officeholder performs the customary duties of the office personally.
predicates.some_responsibilities_assigned_elsewhere: Some responsibilities connected with the office have been assigned to another officer.

issues.definition: If a scheme-modification proceeding concerns a hereditary office, the application did not seek its abolition, the officeholder performs its customary duties, and some responsibilities have merely been assigned elsewhere, restricting the officeholder’s customary remuneration is invalid.
